title: "Table Template: Create your own {gt} table theme"

Creating visually appealing and informative tables is a key aspect of data presentation, and the `gt` package in R provides powerful tools for this purpose. In this post, we will walk through creating a customizable table template using gt. By following these steps, you can easily create tables that are both functional and aesthetically pleasing, tailored to your specific needs.

## Load Required Libraries

First, ensure that you have the `gt` package loaded. All function used below are from `gt` package, except the data setup which I showed where it comes from. 

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# install.packages("gt")        Run only once if don't have the package installed
library(gt)
```


## Prepare Your Data

For this example, we'll use the iris dataset and select a subset of it. We'll group the data by species and take the first two entries from each group.


```{r}
tbl <- iris |> 
        dplyr::mutate(Species = stringr::str_to_title(Species)) |> 
        dplyr::group_by(Species) |> 
        dplyr::slice_head(n = 2) |>
        dplyr::ungroup() |> 
        gt()

tbl
```

## Add a Header
Next, add a title and subtitle to your table for better context and readability.

```{r}
tbl <- tbl |> 
        tab_header(
                title = "Main Title",
                subtitle = "Subtitle"
        )

tbl
```

## Style the Header

Apply styling to the header to make it stand out. Here, we set the text color to blue and make it bold.


```{r}
tbl <- tbl |> 
        tab_style(
                style = cell_text(color = "blue", 
                                  weight = "bold"),
                locations = cells_title(groups = "title")
        )

tbl
```

## Style the Body
To enhance readability, apply a background color to alternating rows in the table body.


```{r}
tbl <- tbl |> 
               tab_style(
                style = cell_fill(color = "grey90"),
                locations = cells_body(rows = seq(1, 6, 2))
        )

tbl
```

## Adjust Table Options
Customize the table width, column label background color, and heading alignment to suit your design preferences.


```{r}
tbl <- tbl |>
        tab_options(
                table.width = pct(100),
                column_labels.background.color = "steelblue",
                heading.align = "left")

tbl
```

## Add Spanners
If your table has grouped columns, add spanners to better organize and present these groups.



```{r}
tbl <- tbl |> 
        tab_spanner_delim(".")

tbl
```

## Style Column Labels and Spanners
Ensure that your column labels and spanners are easily distinguishable by applying bold text and adjusting the size for spanners.

```{r}
tbl <- tbl |> 
        tab_style(
                style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
                locations = cells_column_labels()
        ) |> 
        tab_style(
                style = cell_text(weight = "bold",
                                  size = "medium"),
                locations = cells_column_spanners()
        )

tbl
```


## Reorder Columns
Finally, adjust the order of your columns as needed. In this example, we move the "Species" column to the start.


```{r}
tbl <- tbl |> 
        cols_move_to_start("Species")

tbl
```
